title: Judges 1:16–21
context: The children of the Kenite, Moses’ brother-in-law, go up from the city of palm trees with Judah into the wilderness of Judah, south of Arad, and live with the people. Judah then goes with Simeon, strikes the Canaanites of Zephath, and utterly destroys the city; it is called Hormah. Judah also takes Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, with their borders. The LORD was with Judah and drove out the inhabitants of the hill country, but “he could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.” Hebron is given to Caleb, as Moses had said, and Caleb drives out the three sons of Anak. Benjamin, however, did not drive out the Jebusites who inhabited Jerusalem; they dwell with Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day. Both traditions read a mixed record: real help and real success stand beside failure to finish the work. The “he could not” of verse 19 and the Jerusalem notices in verses 8 and 21 are disputed in the details and should be handled as interpretive questions, not as consensus and not as an Arminian–Reformed contrast. The refrain that a tribe did not drive the inhabitants out is shared ground of incomplete obedience, not a map quarrel between the two traditions.

verses.text: The children of the Kenite, Moses’ brother-in-law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which is in the south of Arad; and they went and lived with the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of the Kenite, “Moses’ brother-in-law,” went up out of the city of palm trees with Judah into the wilderness of Judah, in the south of Arad, and lived with the people. The WEB calls the Kenite Moses’ brother-in-law; the note should follow that wording rather than a different family title.

Arminian readers hear a clan related to Moses settling alongside Judah, a peaceful going-up in the same south country. The “city of palm trees” is commonly identified with Jericho; that identification is widespread, not a point this verse itself names.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the Kenites’ move as a companion settlement with Judah, not as one more battle notice. They leave the city of palm trees for the wilderness south of Arad and live with the people.

Both traditions receive the verse as an allied family finding a place in Judah’s south, without inventing a contrast over the geography or the kinship term.

verses.text: Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they struck the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. The name of the city was called Hormah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah went with Simeon his brother, struck the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. The name of the city was called Hormah.

Arminian readers hear the brothers keeping the mutual word of verse 3. The city is devoted to destruction and renamed; the verse reports a completed stroke in Simeon’s sphere, not a debate over the devoted destruction between the two traditions.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Judah and Simeon act together, and that the city is utterly destroyed and called Hormah. The new name marks the destruction the narrator has just recorded.

Both traditions take the notice as a fulfilled joint campaign, shared ground, without turning the fate of the city into a party contrast.

verses.text: Also Judah took Gaza with its border, and Ashkelon with its border, and Ekron with its border.
verses.arminianNotes:
Also Judah took Gaza with its border, and Ashkelon with its border, and Ekron with its border. Three coastal cities, with their territory, are said to have been taken.

Arminian readers hear a further success, and they also notice that later in this book and in the books of Samuel these places appear as Philistine strongholds. Many readers therefore take the taking as limited or short-lived rather than a lasting occupation; that is a common way of holding the texts together, not a demonstrated consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to ignore either this verse or the later picture of these cities. How a taking here relates to verse 19, and to later Philistine control, is discussed in both traditions.

Neither tradition makes the geography itself a fork. The verse states a taking of Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron; the lasting hold is a question the wider narrative raises.

verses.text: The LORD was with Judah, and drove out the inhabitants of the hill country; for he could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD was with Judah, and drove out the inhabitants of the hill country; for he could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.” The first clause credits the LORD’s presence and the driving out of the hill country.

Arminian readers, with most readers of both traditions, take the “he” who could not drive out the valley as Judah, not as the LORD. Iron chariots became the occasion of a real failure to finish the work, not proof that God was powerless. The people remain responsible for what they did not complete.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise will not read the verse as a limit on the LORD’s power. “The LORD was with Judah” stands; the inability in the valley is most often read as Judah’s, in the face of iron chariots, not as God’s. Presence in the hill country did not make the valley automatic.

Both traditions reject any implication that the LORD could not do what he willed. The failure is Israel’s incomplete obedience, shared ground, not a contrast over divine weakness.

verses.text: They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he drove the three sons of Anak out of there.
verses.arminianNotes:
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he drove the three sons of Anak out of there. The earlier word is kept, and Caleb does what verse 10 had begun to report.

Arminian readers hear a promise honored in a particular man. Moses had said this, the people give Hebron, and Caleb actually drives the three sons of Anak out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same fidelity to Moses’ word. The Anakim who had once made the spies afraid are driven out by the man who had trusted that word.

Both traditions take the verse as the keeping of an earlier command and as Caleb’s success at Hebron, shared ground with verse 10.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin didn’t drive out the Jebusites who inhabited Jerusalem, but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Benjamin “didn’t drive out” the Jebusites who inhabited Jerusalem; the Jebusites dwell with Benjamin in Jerusalem “to this day.” The refrain of not driving out now falls on Benjamin and on this city.

Arminian readers hear a lasting failure, set beside verse 8, where Judah took Jerusalem and set it on fire. The two notices have long been held together in more than one way—a temporary capture, a success that did not become lasting occupation, or different parts or stages of the city—and no one of those readings should be called the consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let both verses stand. Jerusalem lay in the sphere of Judah and Benjamin; verse 21 says the Jebusites were not driven out and still dwelt there when the narrator wrote “to this day.” That phrase marks the writer’s own time; it does not, by itself, fix a date.

Both traditions treat the tension with verse 8 as an interpretive problem, not as a fork between Arminian and Reformed readings, and they take the failure to drive the Jebusites out as shared ground of incomplete obedience.
